lessons.title: Planning and allocating work over two weeks
lessons.html:
Thinking ahead for two weeks

In this workplace module you lead a team for two weeks. That means looking beyond today. Over two weeks a broiler flock can go from day-old chicks to mid grow-out, a house can be depleted and cleaned, or a layer flock can go through vaccinations and a feed change. Plan the work so that nothing important is missed.

Step 1: List the work

Start with the production calendar from your manager. Write down:

  • Daily tasks: house walks, water and feed checks, mortality, egg collection, records, footbaths.
  • Scheduled tasks: vaccinations, weighing, chick placement, catching, feed deliveries, litter top-up, cleaning out.
  • Maintenance tasks: fan belts, drinker cleaning, generator tests, rodent bait checks.

Step 2: Know your team

Note who is available each day, allowing for days off and leave. Know each person's skills. Who can operate the tractor for litter removal? Who is trained for vaccination? Who is new and needs to work with an experienced person?

Step 3: Build a roster

Make a simple two-week roster that shows each person, each day and their main house or task. Keep the same workers on the same houses where possible. This is good for biosecurity and helps workers get to know their birds. Plan extra hands for big days such as placement or catching.

Step 4: Check resources

Make sure PPE, disinfectant, vaccines, tools and fuel will be on hand when needed. Order early. A vaccination day without vaccine in the fridge is a failed plan.

Step 5: Share the plan

Put the roster on the notice board and go through it with the team at the start of the week. Ask for questions and changes, such as a worker with a clinic appointment.

lessons.title: Directing the team and handling day-to-day issues
lessons.html:
Leading the team each day

A plan only works if the team carries it out well. Directing a team means giving clear instructions, checking the work, solving problems and keeping people motivated and safe.

The morning briefing

Hold a short briefing of five to ten minutes each morning. Cover:

  • what happened yesterday, including any problems found
  • today's tasks and who does what
  • any special job, such as a vaccination or feed change
  • a safety reminder, for example lifting feed bags correctly or wearing dust masks during clean-out

Checking work

Walk the houses during the day. Check drinkers, feeders, footbaths and records. When work is not up to standard, tell the worker privately, show the correct way and check again later. Give praise in public when work is done well.

Handling changes and problems

Things go wrong: a worker is sick, a fan breaks, the chick delivery is early. Stay calm and re-plan. Move people to the most urgent work, which is always bird welfare first. Tell the manager about anything you cannot solve, such as a large mortality increase or a broken generator.

People issues

Treat everyone fairly and with respect. Do not shout at or embarrass workers. If a worker is often late or does not follow rules, record the facts and discuss it with your manager, who will follow the farm's disciplinary procedure. Listen to workers' ideas; they often know the house best.

Safety

The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires safe work. Make sure workers wear the right PPE, use correct lifting, keep hands away from moving augers and fans, and report injuries. Keep the first aid box stocked and know who is the trained first aider on site.

Reviewing the two weeks

At the end, compare what was planned with what was done. Note what worked, what did not and what you will change next time. Share this with your manager.

Key points

  • Plan two weeks ahead using the production calendar.
  • Match tasks to workers' skills and availability.
  • Keep workers on the same houses for biosecurity.
  • Brief the team daily and check work during the day.
  • Put bird welfare first when re-planning, and review the period at the end.
